## 2. What the Nebraska library actually puts into the genome

Our strains come from the **Nebraska Transposon Mutant Library (NTML)**
[(Fey et al. 2013, mBio)](https://doi.org/10.1128/mBio.00537-12). Knowing what
is inserted explains a lot.

The transposon is **bursa aurealis**, a *mariner*-family element:

| property | value |
|---|---|
| length | **3,237 bp** including the terminal inverted repeats |
| carries | **`ermB`** (erythromycin resistance – how the mutants are selected) and **`gfp`** |
| delivered by | plasmid **pBursa** (7,383 bp, temperature-sensitive) |
| transposase | from a second plasmid, **pFA545** (also temperature-sensitive) |
| after mutagenesis | both plasmids are removed by growth at 45 °C; only the transposon stays |

Our two strains have catalogue numbers **NE217** (*stk1*) and **NE1919**
(*stp1*) – the same two that Prust et al. 2021 used, which is handy, because we
can compare results directly.

The insertion coordinates come from the
[NTML insertion map](https://ntml.unmc.edu/tninsertionmap):

```{r insertions}
TRANSPOSON_INSERTIONS
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The one thing to take from this table
3,237 bp is **long**. Our two genes are only 744 bp (*stp1*) and 1,995 bp
(*stk1*). The insert is bigger than the gene it lands in.
:::

## 3. Exercise: where exactly does the insertion land?

The table gives a position in the genome. Turn it into something biological:
*which amino acid of the protein does the transposon interrupt?*

Fill in the three missing lines. You need: the position inside the coding
sequence, the codon number, and the length of the protein in amino acids.
(Remember a codon is 3 nucleotides, and the last codon is the stop codon.)

```{r where, eval = FALSE}
insertions <- TRANSPOSON_INSERTIONS |>
  mutate(
    cds_length  = cds_end - cds_start + 1,
    protein_aa  = ___,                       # amino acids (mind the stop codon)
    nt_into_cds = ___,                       # how far into the gene, in nucleotides
    codon       = ___,                       # which codon is hit
    percent     = round(100 * nt_into_cds / cds_length)
  )
insertions |> select(short_name, ntml_id, protein_aa, nt_into_cds, codon, percent)
```

> *Your answer:* for each mutant – which residue is hit, and how far into the
> protein is that, as a percentage?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check your numbers (open after you computed yours)

```{r where-solution}
insertions <- TRANSPOSON_INSERTIONS |>
  mutate(
    cds_length  = cds_end - cds_start + 1,
    protein_aa  = cds_length %/% 3 - 1,
    nt_into_cds = insertion_pos - cds_start + 1,
    codon       = (nt_into_cds + 2) %/% 3,
    percent     = round(100 * nt_into_cds / cds_length)
  )
insertions |> select(short_name, ntml_id, protein_aa, nt_into_cds, codon, percent)
```

So: *stk1* is hit at **codon 46 of 664** (7 % into the gene), but *stp1* at
**codon 189 of 247** – **76 %** of the way through.

That asymmetry matters. The NTML only kept mutants where the transposon landed
"close to the 5′ end" of a gene, and NE1919 is a clear exception.
:::

## 4. A prediction you can actually test

Here is the point of this notebook. A transposon at codon 189 of 247 splits
Stp1 into two parts:

* residues **1–188** are still in frame behind the native promoter,
* residues **189–247** are separated from their start codon by 3.2 kb of
  foreign DNA and **cannot be made**.

The DEA works on **protein-level** numbers – one value per protein per sample,
summarised over all its peptides. That summary cannot see this. But the
**peptides** can.

> *Your answer:* before you look – if a truncated Stp1 (residues 1–188) were
> produced in the `stp` mutant, which peptides would you still expect to find,
> and which not? And what would you expect if NO protein at all is made?

## 5. The peptide layer

`read_peptides()` gives you the table the DEA was built from, *before* peptides
were rolled up into proteins. Each row is one peptide in one sample, with its
position in the protein.

```{r peptides}
pep <- read_peptides()
pep |> filter(locus_tag == "B7H15_06350") |> select(peptide_plain, protein_start, protein_end, sample, intensity) |> head(4)
```

Now draw the map. Each bar is a peptide, placed where it sits in the protein;
darker means detected in more of the 9 samples of that genotype.

```{r coverage-stp, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
plot_peptide_coverage("B7H15_06350", pep, insertion_codon = insertions$codon[insertions$short_name == "Stp1"])
```

```{r coverage-stk, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
plot_peptide_coverage("B7H15_06355", pep, insertion_codon = insertions$codon[insertions$short_name == "Stk1"])
```

And the same thing as a table – peptides detected before vs. after the
insertion point, per genotype:

```{r sides}
sides <- insertions |>
  select(short_name, locus_tag, codon) |>
  left_join(pep, by = "locus_tag", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(side = case_when(protein_end   < codon ~ "before insertion",
                          protein_start > codon ~ "after insertion",
                          TRUE                  ~ "spans it")) |>
  group_by(short_name, genotype, side) |>
  summarise(distinct_peptides = n_distinct(peptide_plain[!is.na(intensity)]),
            total_detections  = sum(!is.na(intensity)), .groups = "drop")
sides |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = genotype,
                            values_from = c(distinct_peptides, total_detections))
```

> *Your answer:* does the `stp` column fit "truncated protein", "no protein at
> all", or neither? Name the single strongest piece of evidence, and then name
> the weakest point of your own argument.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What we see (open after you wrote your answer)

For **Stp1**, the peptides that lie *after* codon 189 are found in essentially
every `anc` and `stk` sample (24 and 23 detections) and almost never in `stp`
(**1** detection, in a single run). The two that sit furthest downstream –
`EGTIEDHGDQLMQLALDNHSK` (residues 212–232) and `DNVTFILAAIEGDKV` (233–247) –
are absent from all nine `stp` samples. A handful of peptides from the front of
the protein still turn up in `stp`, but only in one to three samples each.

That is the signature you predicted for a truncation – and it explains the
**erratic protein values**: the protein-level number was mixing N-terminal
peptides that sometimes appear with C-terminal peptides that never do.

Be honest about the limits, though: the few remaining N-terminal detections are
sporadic, which is not what a stable, well-expressed truncated protein would
look like. "Truncated and then degraded" and "spill-over between runs in DIA"
both remain on the table. A good next step is to check *which* runs those
detections come from.

For **Stk1**, `stk` and `stp` are simply empty. Note that the absence of an
N-terminal fragment proves little here: residues 1–45 produce almost no
detectable tryptic peptides even in the wild type (look at the `anc` panel).
:::

## 6. Why the `stp` mutant also loses Stk1

Now the first mystery. Look at where the two genes sit:

```{r operon}
find_protein(c("B7H15_06350", "B7H15_06355")) |> select(locus_tag, product, location)

TRANSPOSON_INSERTIONS |>
  summarise(stp1_ends = max(cds_end[short_name == "Stp1"]),
            stk1_starts = min(cds_start[short_name == "Stk1"]),
            gap_bp = stk1_starts - stp1_ends - 1)
```

> *Your answer:* what is the gap between the end of *stp1* and the start of
> *stk1*? What does a negative number mean? And what does it tell you about how
> the two genes are transcribed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself
The genes **overlap by 4 bp** – *stp1* ends at 1,233,038 and *stk1* starts at
1,233,035. Overlapping stop/start codons are a hallmark of genes in one
**operon**, transcribed as a single mRNA and translationally coupled.

Drop 3.2 kb of foreign DNA into *stp1*, only 174 bp upstream of the *stk1*
start, and transcription will very likely not read through into *stk1*. This is
a **polar effect**, and it is exactly what the proteome shows.

Fey et al. state plainly that they *"did not perform studies to assess the
possibility of polar effects"* and that every phenotype must be confirmed by
independent genetic means. Our `stp` strain is a concrete example of why.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Consequence for the whole course
Every contrast involving `stp` – `stp_vs_anc`, `stp_vs_stk`, and every
`interaction_stp_*` – compares the wild type against a strain that has lost
**both** the phosphatase **and** (most of) the kinase. It is not a clean
"phosphatase-only" mutant. Say this in your report, and say it whenever you
interpret an `stp` result.
:::

## 7. Something that is missing from our search

A thought that follows from section 2: if the transposon carries `ermB` and
`gfp`, and those genes are expressed, then **ErmB protein should be in the
mutant samples** – and in the wild type it cannot be.

That would be a beautiful positive control: a protein that is present *because*
of the transposon rather than absent because of it.

Is it in our data?

```{r ermb}
#| message: true
# Is there anything resembling ErmB in the search database?
find_protein(c("erythromycin", "rRNA adenine N-6", "macrolide"))
nrow(read_annotation())   # how many entries the database has in total
```

GFP is a different story – it *is* in the FASTA, but only because the FGCZ
contaminant list happens to contain it (entry `zz_Y-FGCZCont00258_`, the
*Aequorea victoria* protein). So it was searchable. Was it found?

```{r gfp}
pep_all <- read_peptides(drop_contaminants = FALSE)
pep_all |>
  filter(protein_key == "zz_Y-FGCZCont00258_", !is.na(intensity)) |>
  nrow()
```

> *Your answer:* can a search engine ever report a protein that is not in the
> FASTA file it searched against? What does that mean for the question "is ErmB
> there?"

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The answer, and what we are doing about it
No. A database search can only assign spectra to sequences that are **in the
FASTA**. `ermB` is not in ours, so its spectra – if any were recorded – were
either left unassigned or forced onto some other sequence. "Not found" here
means "never looked for".

GFP *is* in the FASTA, as a contaminant entry, and was **not** detected. That
is weak evidence against GFP expression (the transposon carries a yeast
codon-optimised *gfp* whose protein sequence may differ from the entry we have).

So the honest answer is: **we cannot say yet.** The data would have to be
re-searched against an extended FASTA. The repository contains a proposal for
that in [`reference/`](../reference/) – see the README there. This is a real
experiment, not a classroom exercise, and the lecturer has the raw files.
:::

> mutant? Which of the two is a clean knock-out? What must a reader of your
> report be told before they believe an `stp` result?

### Discussion prompts

* NE1919 sits at 76 % of *stp1*, against the library's own selection rule. Does
  that make it a worse mutant – or could a truncated phosphatase be *worse than
  useless*, for example still binding its substrate without dephosphorylating it?
* The pre-experiment growth curves said the `stp` strain copes slightly
  **better** with PASN than the wild type. Does that still make sense if `stp`
  is really a double mutant, given that `stk` copes clearly **worse**?
* Prust et al. derived Stk1 substrates by looking for sites that go **up** in
  the *stp1* mutant, assuming Stk1 is still active there. What does our result
  do to that assumption – for their paper, and for the group working on topic g?
* How would you prove the polar effect properly, with a wet-lab experiment?
